title: Was, were, and once upon a time
seoTitle: Turkmen past of to be, eken and -ypdyr
intro: This unit is about how the past is told. First, **was** and **were**: the past of **to be** on nouns and adjectives (*talypdym*, *öýdedik*), with *bardy*, *ýokdy* and *däldi*. Then two ways of telling what you didn't see for yourself: *eken*, for something you have found out or heard (*Ol mugallym eken*), and a first look at `-(Y)pdYr` (*Ol gelipdir*). Both are how Turkmen folk tales are told, from their first words: *Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken…*

sections.title: I was, there was: the past of to be

blocks.text: To say what someone or something **was**, add `-dY` to the noun, adjective or place word, then the same endings as the past of verbs ([A2 unit 1](a2-u01)): *talyp* → *talypdym*, I was a student; *öýde* → *öýdedik*, we were at home; *ýadaw* → *ýadawdy*, she was tired. After a vowel `-dY` joins directly: *çagadym*, I was a child.

rows.en: he or she was a student
he or she was at home
you were at home (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **The ending is always there.** In the present, everyday **to be** has no ending (*Men talyp*). In the past it always has one: *Men talypdym*. So the pronoun can be left out: *Talypdym*, I was a student. With *olar*, you will also see the plural first: *Olar talyplardy*.

**There was, there wasn't.** *bar* and *ýok* take `-dY` too: *bardy* (there was), *ýokdy* (there wasn't). With the locative of a person they say what someone **had**, as in [A1 unit 9](a1-u09): *Mende pul ýokdy*, I had no money; *Onuň bir iti bardy*, he had a dog.
**Wasn't.** *däl* takes the ending: *däldim, däldiň, däldi, däldik, däldiňiz, däldiler*. *Men ýadaw däldim*, I wasn't tired; *Ol öýde däldi*, she wasn't at home.

rows.en: he or she wasn't a student

blocks.text: **Questions.** Here the particle comes **before** `-dY`, straight after the noun: *talyp-my-dy-ň?* Were you a student? *Öýdemidi?* Was she at home? *Barmydy?* Was there any? For **wasn't**, after *däl*: *Talyp dälmidiň?* Weren't you a student?

rows.en: Was he or she a student?

items.en: There were a lot of people at the wedding.
In my childhood I was very happy.
I had no money on me.

blocks.title: Or with bolmak
blocks.text: *bolmak* in the past says much the same about where someone was: *Men düýn öýde boldum*, I was at home yesterday; *Sen Maryda bolduňmy?*, have you been to Mary? Use `-dY` on the noun for what someone or something was like: *Men çagadym*, *Howa sowukdy*.

blocks.title: The particle moves
blocks.text: With verbs the question particle comes last: *geldiňmi?* With nouns in the past it comes before `-dY`: *talypmydyň?*, not `talypdyňmy`. And never drop the ending in the past: *Men talypdym*, not `Men talypdy`.

sections.title: So it is, I hear: eken

blocks.text: *eken*, written as a separate word after a noun, adjective or place word, shows that you didn't know this until now: you have just found it out, or someone told you. *Ol mugallym* states a fact: he's a teacher. *Ol mugallym eken* says **so he's a teacher**, **he's a teacher, it turns out**, or **he's a teacher, I'm told**. English needs extra words; Turkmen has *eken*.

items.en: There's a café here, I see.
Merdan isn't at home, it turns out.
His grandfather was a doctor, I'm told.
This book is interesting, it turns out.

blocks.text: Notice that *eken* can be about now (the café is here) or about the past (the grandfather was a doctor). What it marks is not the time but how you know: by discovering it or hearing it. With *bardy* you remember a café that was there; with *bar eken* you have just learned of it.

**Once upon a time.** Turkmen folk tales, *ertekiler*, open with *Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken*: literally **there was one, there wasn't one**, the Turkmen **once upon a time**. The teller wasn't there, so the tale goes on with *eken*: *Bir obada bir garry adam bar eken. Onuň üç ogly bar eken.* (In a village there was an old man. He had three sons.)

lines.en: No, it's near, it turns out.

blocks.text: In this unit *eken* is used positive only, about **he, she, it**, **they** and things. It also goes with *däl* and with the other persons, and after verbs; those uses come in [B1 unit 3](b1-u03).

blocks.title: A word of its own
blocks.text: *eken* is written apart: *mugallym eken*, not `mugallymeken`. It takes no `-dY`: **there was, I hear** is *bar eken*, not `bardy eken`.

sections.title: A first look at -(Y)pdYr: it has happened, I see

blocks.text: For an **action** you didn't see happen but know about from its result or from someone else, Turkmen uses `-(Y)pdYr`. *Ol geldi* is the plain past: he came. *Ol gelipdir* means **he's come** when you see his shoes by the door, or **he came, they say**, when someone has told you.

Build it in two steps. First `-(Y)p`: *-yp* or *-ip* after a consonant, just *-p* after a vowel: *gel-ip*, *oka-p*. Then `-dYr`: *-dyr* or *-dir*. So *gelipdir*, *okapdyr*. For **they**, add *-lAr*: *gelipdirler*.

blocks.title: *gelmek*: he has come, they have come

rows.en: he or she has come (I see, I'm told)
they have come (I see, I'm told)
he or she has read (I see, I'm told)
they have read (I see, I'm told)

blocks.text: The rules you know apply to `-(Y)p`. It rounds in the second syllable (*görüpdir*, *bolupdyr*), and the third stays *y* or *i* (*-dyr*, *-dir*). A stem's final *e* becomes *ä* before *-p*: *işläpdir*. And the *t*-verbs soften before its vowel: *gidipdir*, *edipdir*, *aýdypdyr*.

items.en: It has rained. (The ground is wet.)
Merjen has gone to Mary, I hear.
The guests have already arrived, I see.
The child has fallen asleep, I see.

items.tk: Bir gün tilki bir möjegi görüpdir.
items.seg: Bir gün tilki bir möjeg|i gör|üp|dir.
items.en: One day the fox saw a wolf.

blocks.text: The last example is how tales tell their story: the teller didn't see it, so the actions come in `-(Y)pdYr`, and the scene is set with *eken*. *Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken, bir patyşa bar eken. Bir gün patyşa bir düýş görüpdir…* (Once upon a time there was a king. One day the king had a dream…)

blocks.title: The plain past or -(Y)pdYr?
blocks.text: Say *geldi* for what you saw or simply state; say *gelipdir* when you see the result or pass on what you heard. In this unit you meet only **he, she, it** and **they**, positive. The other persons, the negative and questions come in [B1 unit 3](b1-u03).

blocks.title: One word
blocks.text: *gelipdir* is one word: the stem, *-ip* and *-dir*. Don't split it (`gelip dir`) and don't drop the *p*: `geldir` is not a past form.

summary: **Was, were**: noun or adjective + `-dY` + *-m, -ň, —, -k, -ňYz, -lAr*: *talypdym, öýdediň, sowukdy*. In the past the ending is never dropped.
*bardy* (there was), *ýokdy* (there wasn't), *däldim* (I wasn't). Questions put `-mY` before `-dY`: *talypmydyň?*, *barmydy?*
*eken*, a separate word, marks what you have just found out or heard: *Ol mugallym eken*.
`-(Y)pdYr` tells an action you didn't see, known from its result or from others: *Ol gelipdir*, *Ýagyş ýagypdyr*; for **they**, *-lAr*.
Tales begin *Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken* and go on with *eken* and `-(Y)pdYr`.
